findings.quote: We study the out-of-fold filter, which uses only the noisy training set: it drops each sample whose label disagrees with a logistic regression fit on the cross-validation folds that exclude it, then refits once, with no confidence threshold.

We compare it with logistic regression and a multilayer perceptron trained on all given labels, using two small datasets (digits, breast cancer) with clean labels and synthetic symmetric noise at two rates.
Never told the noise rate, the filter removes a few percent of a clean training set but a large, mostly mislabeled share of a noisy one, catching most flipped labels.
The refit model beats unfiltered logistic regression in all but one noisy run and costs only a fraction of a point of mean accuracy on clean labels.
On seed means, it wins back much of the accuracy that noise costs logistic regression, but only a small part on breast cancer at the higher noise rate.
It also discards correctly labeled samples and does not restore clean-label accuracy.
Logistic regression filters its own training labels with out-of-fold predictions.

(a) A logistic regression fit on the other cross-validation folds predicts each training sample (1), the prediction is compared with the given label (2), mismatches are dropped (3), and the model is refit once (4).

(b) Share of the training set removed, split into mislabeled and correctly labeled samples.
Black ticks mark the mislabeled share of the whole training set.

(c) Test accuracy of ours and of logistic regression trained on all given labels; gray lines mark logistic regression trained on clean labels (the clean-label reference).
Bars in (b) and (c) are means over 5\src{n_seeds} seeds.
In (c), error bars are sd, dots are seeds, and the accuracy axis does not start at zero.
Under noise, ours has the higher mean, although the seeds do not establish the gain on breast cancer at 20\%\src{noise_rate_low} noise.
A gap to the gray line remains, largest on breast cancer at 40\%\src{noise_rate_high} noise.

findings.quote: A practitioner who trains a linear classifier on cheaply gathered labels can expect some of them to be wrong, without knowing which or how many.

On both datasets we study, digits and breast cancer, symmetric label noise (training labels randomly replaced by other classes) lowers the test accuracy of logistic regression, more so at the higher noise rate (Fig.~\ref{fig:teaser}c, logistic regression bars against the gray lines).

Common repairs ask for something this practitioner may not have: a clean validation set, a hand-chosen confidence threshold, or a noise rate that sets how many samples to drop and must itself be estimated~\citep{song2023learning}.
findings.fix: Neither the ledger nor the verified summary of the survey backs the validation set, the threshold or the drop count. Replace with: "Some repairs rely on quantities this practitioner does not know, such as class corruption probabilities~\citep{patrini2017making} or the noise rate~\citep{liu2016classification}, which then have to be estimated."

findings.quote: The out-of-fold filter asks only for the noisy training set (Fig.~\ref{fig:teaser}a).
It checks every label against the prediction of a logistic regression fit on the cross-validation folds that exclude that sample, drops the sample if the two disagree, and refits once on the rest.
Nothing fixes in advance how many samples go: \emph{a linear classifier can filter its own training labels without being told how many are wrong}.

The filter is the simplest member of the classification filtering family~\citep{brodley1999identifying} and a close relative of confident learning~\citep{northcutt2021confident}; we claim no new method.

findings.quote: On two small datasets, with clean labels and symmetric noise, we make three contributions:
\textbf{A filter that needs only the noisy labels.}

findings.quote: We describe a one-pass out-of-fold filter with which logistic regression prunes its own training labels, using no clean validation set, noise-rate estimate or confidence threshold.

We show that it removes a few percent of a clean training set but a large share of a noisy one, mostly mislabeled and including most flipped labels, although correctly labeled samples go too (Fig.~\ref{fig:teaser}b).

We find that the refit model beats unfiltered logistic regression in all but one noisy run (Fig.~\ref{fig:paired_gain}), costs little on clean labels and on seed means wins back much of the lost accuracy, but only a small part on breast cancer at the higher noise rate (Fig.~\ref{fig:teaser}c).
Classification filtering removes training samples that held-out classifiers misclassify.
\citet{brodley1999identifying} built such filters from one learning algorithm or from several that vote.
Confident learning~\citep{northcutt2021confident} combines pruning with an estimate, from probabilistic thresholds, of how given and true labels are jointly distributed.
We study the plainest version, with logistic regression as the only learner and no threshold, and measure what it drops on clean as well as noisy labels.
findings.fix: No ledger claim ranks filters by plainness. Change "We study the plainest version" to "We study a plain version".

findings.quote: Co-teaching~\citep{han2018coteaching} trains two networks that each select possibly clean samples in every mini-batch for the other to learn from.
Related methods use per-sample losses to find likely clean samples during training~\citep{wei2020combating,li2020dividemix}.
Our filter acts once before the final fit, uses only logistic regression and takes no drop rate.
Surveys cover types of label noise and ways to learn despite it~\citep{frenay2014classification,song2023learning}.
Loss correction adjusts the loss using class corruption probabilities, which can be estimated from data~\citep{patrini2017making}.
We change the training set instead, estimate no noise parameters and test only symmetric noise.
The filter changes which samples logistic regression is fit on.
The base model $f_D$ (standardization, then logistic regression, both fit on $D$) maps a feature vector to a class.
The logistic regression baseline is $f_D$ with all given labels.
We shuffle $D$ into $K$ cross-validation folds~\citep{stone1974crossvalidatory}, stratified on the given labels, and write $D_{k(i)}$ for the fold that contains sample $i$.
Its out-of-fold prediction is the class $\hat{y}_i = f_{D \setminus D_{k(i)}}(x_i)$.
This model, standardization included, never saw sample $i$, so it cannot have memorized a wrong label for it.
We keep a sample only if its out-of-fold prediction equals its given label.
The refit model $f_{D_{\mathrm{keep}}}$ is a new standardization and logistic regression fit on this set.
The filter makes one pass over hard predictions, with no confidence threshold or per-class rule (Fig.~\ref{fig:teaser}a).
It needs no clean validation set or noise-rate estimate, and the number of drops is the number of disagreements.
We fix $K$ and the inverse regularization strength $C$ without tuning (Section~\ref{sec:setup}).

We use two small datasets from scikit-learn~\citep{pedregosa2012scikitlearn}: digits (1,257\src{n_train_digits} training and 540\src{n_test_digits} test samples) and breast cancer~\citep{mangasarian1995breast} (398\src{n_train_breast} and 171\src{n_test_breast}).

Symmetric noise independently flips each training label, with probability equal to the noise rate (20\%\src{noise_rate_low} or 40\%\src{noise_rate_high}), to a different class drawn uniformly at random.
We also train on clean labels.
Test labels stay clean.
The filter uses $K = 5\src{filter_folds}$ folds.
We compare it with logistic regression and an untuned multilayer perceptron (MLP), both trained on all given labels.
On clean labels, this logistic regression is the clean-label reference.
The MLP has one hidden layer of 64\src{mlp_hidden} units, runs at most 500\src{mlp_max_iter} iterations and otherwise keeps library defaults.
Every logistic regression uses $C = 1\src{logreg_c}$.
All methods standardize features and share each run's split and noisy labels.
We report test accuracy and, for the filter, the share of the training set removed, drop precision (the share of drops whose label we flipped) and drop recall (the share of flipped labels dropped).
Pre-existing label errors are not counted.
The share of lost accuracy won back is a ratio of seed means: ours minus noisy-label logistic regression, divided by the clean-label reference minus noisy-label logistic regression.
Each of 5\src{n_seeds} seeds per setting sets the stratified split, noise, folds and MLP initialization.
Two-sided $t$-tests across seeds are paired between methods or noise rates, or compare a share with one half.

\subsection{Under noise, most dropped samples are mislabeled}
The number of drops adapts to the labels.
The filter is never told the noise rate, yet how much it removes grows with the noise (Fig.~\ref{fig:teaser}b, Table~\ref{tab:drops}).
With clean labels it removes only 3.5\%\src{drop_fraction_digits_noise0} of the training set on digits and 1.9\%\src{drop_fraction_breast_noise0} on breast cancer.
No label is flipped there, so every drop is a correctly labeled sample.
Most flips are caught, at a price.
In every noisy run, drop precision lies between 61\%\src{drop_precision_min} and 81\%\src{drop_precision_max}.
In each noisy setting, it is also far above the mislabeled share of the whole training set.
The filter catches most flipped labels as well, on both datasets and at both noise rates (Table~\ref{tab:drops}).
Correctly labeled samples still make up a sizable minority of the drops, and at the higher rate the filter removes up to about half of the training set.
Heavier noise shifts what is dropped.
At the higher rate, drop recall is lower on both datasets, while drop precision rises on digits and falls on breast cancer.
Breast cancer at this rate also has the lowest drop recall and, on seed means, the smallest share of lost accuracy won back (Table~\ref{tab:drops}).
We observe the two together; our runs do not show that one causes the other.
\subsection{Refitting wins back part of the accuracy lost to noise}
Run by run, ours is more accurate than logistic regression in all noisy runs but one.
Each dot is one seed, with both methods on the same split and given labels, plotted as the test accuracy of ours minus that of logistic regression trained on all given labels.
Bars are means over 5\src{n_seeds} seeds and error bars are sd.
The exception is on breast cancer at 20\%\src{noise_rate_low} noise, the one noisy setting where the mean gain is not established.
On clean labels, both mean gains are slightly below zero.
Filtering beats training on all noisy labels.

It is ahead in 19\src{wins_vs_logreg_noisy} of the 20\src{n_noisy_runs} noisy runs on the same split (Fig.~\ref{fig:paired_gain}).
Its advantage is larger at the higher rate than with clean labels on both datasets, and on digits it also grows from the lower to the higher rate.
On breast cancer at the lower rate, it has the higher mean accuracy, but the seeds do not establish this difference.
Recovery is partial.

On seed means, one pass wins back much of the lost accuracy on digits at both rates and on breast cancer at the lower rate, but only 22.1\%\src{recovered_breast_noise40} on breast cancer at the higher rate (Table~\ref{tab:drops}).
A paired test establishes that more than half is won back only on digits at the lower rate.

findings.quote: Accuracy on breast cancer at the higher rate varies widely between seeds, yet every paired gain there stays above zero (Fig.~\ref{fig:paired_gain}).
The refit model also remains below the clean-label reference at the higher rate on both datasets and on breast cancer at the lower rate.
The MLP gap does not isolate filtering.
The refit model beats the MLP trained on all noisy labels in every noisy run, but plain logistic regression does too, in all 20\src{wins_logreg_vs_mlp_noisy} of these runs.
The MLP also loses more accuracy to noise than logistic regression does (Table~\ref{tab:accuracy}).
Our lead over this untuned MLP is therefore no evidence that filtering beats larger models.
\subsection{On clean labels, the filter costs little}
Discarding correctly labeled samples costs little when the labels are already clean.

The mean paired difference in test accuracy, ours minus logistic regression, is only $-0.2$\src{gain_vs_logreg_digits_noise0} points on digits and $-0.1$\src{gain_vs_logreg_breast_noise0} points on breast cancer (Table~\ref{tab:accuracy}, Fig.~\ref{fig:paired_gain}).
Paired tests across seeds cannot distinguish either difference from zero, which does not show that the two models are equivalent.
The refit model is also not the most accurate option here: the MLP is ahead of it on digits, and on breast cancer the two have nearly equal mean accuracy.
Checking each label against a model that never saw it lets a linear classifier filter its training set using only that set.
In the tested settings, this fixed filter removed mostly mislabeled samples under noise, raised mean test accuracy over logistic regression there and cost little on clean labels.

findings.quote: It still discards correctly labeled samples and wins back the lost accuracy only in part, leaving a gap to the clean-label reference on both datasets at the higher noise rate and on breast cancer at the lower one.
We studied two small datasets, synthetic symmetric noise at two rates, one pass with fixed $K$ and $C$, and one untuned, unfiltered MLP, with seeds that re-split the same data.
Without random-drop or oracle controls, we do not attribute the gain to removing the right samples.
We ran neither co-teaching~\citep{han2018coteaching} nor confident learning~\citep{northcutt2021confident}, compared no other filtering rule and claim no advantage over these methods.
Next steps are these missing runs, class-dependent noise, other rates, and softer or repeated filtering.
